# Physics and Navigation Tool Reference

Complete tool tables for the physics (51 tools) and navigation (15 tools)
domains. Every name below is a registered tool name - pass it to `call_tool`.
See `SKILL.md` in the parent folder for workflows and the RID mental model.

## 2D queries and spaces

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `get_physics_2d_space_direct_state` | Direct state of a 2D space; confirms it is valid, active and in a scene, and lists the available queries. |
| `intersect_physics_2d_ray` | Closest-hit ray cast; `space_rid` may be omitted to auto-detect the edited scene's 2D world inside the editor process (see the note below). |
| `intersect_physics_2d_shape` | All colliders overlapping a shape RID; `transform` places it, `motion` sweeps it. |
| `intersect_physics_2d_point` | All colliders touching a point; `max_results` caps the reply (default 32). |

`intersect_physics_2d_ray` auto-detection resolves the World2D space of the
edited scene root's SubViewport in the editor process. The editor and a running
game are separate processes with independent physics worlds, so coordinates from
the game never hit anything in the editor space. Both the hit and the null reply
carry the queried `space_rid` and an auto_detected flag; cross-check `space_rid`
against `get_physics_2d_space_direct_state` to confirm which space was actually
queried. A null result means the query ran but hit nothing, while a
space_get_direct_state returned null error means the direct state was unavailable
(physics thread running or space locked) - a different failure, not a miss.

## 2D bodies

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `create_physics_2d_body` | Create a server-side 2D body; returns the numeric RID `id` and `is_valid`. |
| `set_physics_2d_body_mode` | 0=static, 1=kinematic, 2=rigid, 3=rigid_linear; only rigid modes respond to forces. |
| `apply_physics_2d_body_force` | Continuous force; optional `position` makes it off-center. |
| `apply_physics_2d_body_impulse` | Instantaneous impulse for jumps/hits; optional off-center `position`. |
| `set_physics_2d_body_state` | Write a field: 0=transform, 1=linear_vel, 2=angular_vel, 3=sleeping, 4=can_sleep. |
| `get_physics_2d_body_state` | Read the same fields back as JSON. |

## 2D joints, areas and shapes

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `create_physics_2d_joint` | Joint between two bodies; `type` "pin", "groove" or "damped_spring". |
| `create_physics_2d_area` | 2D area that detects overlaps and can apply effects such as gravity. |
| `set_physics_2d_area_monitorable` | Whether other areas can monitor this area. |
| `create_physics_2d_circle_shape` | Circle shape RID; NOT assignable to `CollisionShape2D.shape` - server queries only. |
| `set_physics_2d_shape_data` | Size the circle shape, e.g. `data`: `{"radius": 10}`. |

## 3D queries and spaces

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `get_physics_3d_space_direct_state` | Direct state of a 3D space; gateway for 3D queries, fails on inactive spaces. |
| `intersect_physics_3d_ray` | Closest-hit ray cast; `space_rid` required (no auto-detection in 3D). |
| `intersect_physics_3d_shape` | All colliders overlapping a shape RID; optional `transform` and `motion` sweep. |
| `intersect_physics_3d_point` | All colliders at a point; `max_results` caps the reply (default 32). |

## 3D bodies

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `create_physics_3d_body` | Create a server-side 3D body; returns the numeric RID `id` and `is_valid`. |
| `set_physics_3d_body_mode` | 0=static, 1=kinematic, 2=rigid, 3=rigid_linear. |
| `set_physics_3d_body_transform` | Place or teleport the body with a Transform3D (basis array plus origin). |
| `apply_physics_3d_body_force` | Continuous force; rigid modes only. |
| `apply_physics_3d_body_impulse` | Instantaneous impulse; optional off-center `position`. |
| `apply_physics_3d_body_torque` | Rotational torque per axis; no 2D counterpart. |
| `set_physics_3d_body_state` | Write a field: 0=transform, 1=linear_vel, 2=angular_vel, 3=sleeping, 4=can_sleep. |
| `get_physics_3d_body_state` | Read the same fields back as JSON. |
| `set_physics_3d_body_param` | BodyParameter enum: 0=bounce, 1=friction, 2=mass, 3=inertia, 4=center_of_mass, 5=gravity_scale, 6=linear_damp_mode, 7=angular_damp_mode, 8=linear_damp, 9=angular_damp. |
| `set_physics_3d_body_axis_lock` | Bit flags: 1=linear_x, 2=linear_y, 4=linear_z, 8=angular_x, 16=angular_y, 32=angular_z. |
| `add_physics_3d_body_shape` | Attach a shape RID as collision geometry; optional `transform`, `disabled`. |
| `add_physics_3d_body_collision_exception` | Stop colliding with `excepted_body_rid`. |
| `remove_physics_3d_body_collision_exception` | Re-enable collisions; pair with the add tool. |

## 3D shapes and soft bodies

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `create_physics_3d_sphere_shape` | Sphere shape RID; NOT assignable to `CollisionShape3D.shape` - server queries only. |
| `set_physics_3d_shape_data` | Size the sphere shape, e.g. `data`: `{"radius": 0.5}`. |
| `create_physics_3d_soft_body` | Soft body RID that deforms under forces. |
| `set_physics_3d_soft_body_mesh` | Assign the deforming mesh via `mesh_rid`. |

## 3D joints, areas and space solver

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `create_physics_3d_joint` | `type` "pin" (`local_a`/`local_b`), "hinge" (`hinge_a`/`hinge_b`), "slider", "cone_twist" or "generic_6dof" (`ref_a`/`ref_b`); `body_a_rid` required. |
| `set_physics_3d_joint_param` | Tune `solver_priority` and `disable_collision`. |
| `create_physics_3d_area` | 3D area for overlap detection and effects such as gravity and damping. |
| `set_physics_3d_area_param` | AreaParameter enum: 0=gravity_override_mode, 1=gravity, 2=gravity_vector, 3=gravity_is_point, 4=gravity_point_unit_distance, 5=linear_damp_override_mode, 6=linear_damp, 7=angular_damp_override_mode, 8=angular_damp, 9=priority. |
| `set_physics_3d_area_transform` | Place the area's detection volume. |
| `set_physics_3d_area_space` | Attach the area to a space (`space_rid`). |

| Tool | Purpose |

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|

| `set_nav_2d_agent_velocity` | Desired velocity, fed every frame to drive avoidance. |

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|

---
name: godot-autopilot-servers
description: "Godot server-layer RID tools guide: RenderingServer, PhysicsServer and NavigationServer semantics - RID lifecycles and silent failures, physics tick ordering, navigation sync slots and the editor single-thread assumption. Use for server-side drawing, physics simulation or pathfinding."
---

# Godot Server RID Tools

Invocation: use the native MCP tools first; when that channel is down, follow the calling ladder in the godot-autopilot-tools skill (the gda CLI, via bunx, a global install, or the standalone gda binary); with no CLI available, work through its references/manual-fallback.md.

godot-autopilot exposes the engine's server layer directly: `RenderingServer`,
`TextServer`, `PhysicsServer2D`, `PhysicsServer3D`, `NavigationServer2D` and
`NavigationServer3D`. These tools create and drive server-side objects through
RID handles - plain integer ids - instead of scene nodes. Use them for
ray/shape/point queries, server-side simulation, pathfinding setup, custom 2D
drawing, render-only 3D setups, environment post-effects, shaders, and font
shaping measurement.

## The RID mental model

- Every `create_*` tool returns an RID handle. Physics creation tools return an
  object with the numeric `id` and an `is_valid` flag; navigation tools return
  the id as `rid`; render tools return it as `result.rid`. Keep the number and
  pass it as the `rid`/`space_rid`/`map_rid`/`canvas_item_rid` argument of
  follow-up tools.
- Server objects and scene nodes are separate worlds. A body created with
  `create_physics_2d_body` or `create_physics_3d_body` has **no scene node**:
  nothing appears in the editor scene tree and nothing is written to the scene
  file. RIDs live only in the running editor process.
- Bridges connect RIDs to the edited scene: `get_physics_node_rid` (RID of a
  `CollisionObject2D`/`CollisionObject3D` node such as a `RigidBody2D` or
  `CharacterBody3D`); `get_render_canvas_item_rid` (RID of a `CanvasItem` node,
  feeds the `add_render_canvas_item_*` draw tools); `find_render_node_from_rid`
  (reverse lookup: `is_valid` plus a `nodes` array of `node_path`/`type`);
  `get_debug_object_info` (resolve an object id, e.g. a hit's `collider_id`, to
  class, name, `node_path` or `resource_path`).
- **RID shapes are not resources.** The RIDs from `create_physics_2d_circle_shape`
  and `create_physics_3d_sphere_shape` **cannot be assigned to
  `CollisionShape2D.shape` or `CollisionShape3D.shape`** - those properties expect
  a `Shape2D`/`Shape3D` resource. To attach collision geometry to a scene node,
  create a `.tres` via `save_resource` with `class_type`
  "CircleShape2D"/"SphereShape3D" and assign it with `property_set` (`type_hint`
  "Resource"), or assign inside `code_execute`. Use the RID forms only with the
  server tools.
- Several render tools accept RIDs that no tool can create (environments,
  instances, sky/viewport attachments); those must come from external sources
  such as `code_execute`. The tool descriptions call this out.

## Physics queries

2D: start with `get_physics_2d_space_direct_state` - it reports whether the space
is valid, active and attached to a scene, plus the query entry points; queries
fail on inactive spaces.

- `intersect_physics_2d_ray` - closest hit (`position`, `normal`, `collider_id`,
  `rid`, `shape`) or null. `space_rid` may be omitted: the tool auto-detects the
  open editor scene's 2D world.
- `intersect_physics_2d_shape` - all colliders overlapping a shape RID;
  `transform` places it, `motion` sweeps it along a vector.
- `intersect_physics_2d_point` - everything touching one point; `max_results`
  caps the reply (default 32).

3D: same trio, but **`space_rid` is always required** - no auto-detection. Obtain the space
via `code_execute` (e.g. `SceneRoot.get_node("Player").get_world_3d().space`), then confirm
with `get_physics_3d_space_direct_state`.

Shared filters: `collision_mask`, `exclude` (array of RIDs),
`collide_with_bodies`, `collide_with_areas`; rays also take `hit_back_faces` and
`hit_from_inside`. Only the 2D ray auto-detects the space.

## Physics bodies, joints and areas

`create_physics_2d_body` / `create_physics_3d_body` return a RID, then:

- `set_physics_2d_body_mode` / `set_physics_3d_body_mode` - 0=static, 1=kinematic,
  2=rigid, 3=rigid_linear. Only rigid modes respond to forces and impulses.
- `apply_physics_2d_body_force` / `apply_physics_3d_body_force` (continuous) and
  `apply_physics_2d_body_impulse` / `apply_physics_3d_body_impulse` (instantaneous -
  jumps, hits); an optional `position` applies off-center, which adds rotation. 3D adds
  `apply_physics_3d_body_torque` (no 2D counterpart - 2D rotation is scalar).
- `set_physics_2d_body_state` / `get_physics_2d_body_state` (and the 3D pair)
  write and read fields by index: 0=transform, 1=linear_vel, 2=angular_vel,
  3=sleeping, 4=can_sleep.
- 3D extras: `set_physics_3d_body_transform` (place/teleport),
  `set_physics_3d_body_param` (BodyParameter enum 0-9: bounce, friction, mass,
  inertia, center_of_mass, gravity_scale, damp modes and damps),
  `set_physics_3d_body_axis_lock` (bit flags 1=linear_x through 32=angular_z),
  `add_physics_3d_body_shape` (optional `transform`, `disabled`) and the
  collision exception add/remove pair.

Shapes: `create_physics_2d_circle_shape` / `create_physics_3d_sphere_shape`, sized
with `set_physics_2d_shape_data` / `set_physics_3d_shape_data` (`data`:
`{"radius": ...}`). Shape RIDs feed shape queries and `add_physics_3d_body_shape`.

Joints: `create_physics_2d_joint` with `type` "pin" (needs `anchor`), "groove" or
"damped_spring". `create_physics_3d_joint` with "pin", "hinge", "slider",
"cone_twist" or "generic_6dof" - `body_a_rid` required, type-specific transforms
optional. `set_physics_3d_joint_param` tunes `solver_priority` and `disable_collision`.

Areas: `create_physics_2d_area` / `create_physics_3d_area` detect overlaps and
apply effects such as gravity; `set_physics_2d_area_monitorable` /
`set_physics_3d_area_monitorable` control area-to-area monitoring. 3D adds
`set_physics_3d_area_param` (AreaParameter enum 0-9), `set_physics_3d_area_transform`
and `set_physics_3d_area_space`.

Spaces: `set_physics_3d_space_solver_iterations`, `set_physics_3d_space_solver_params`
and `set_physics_3d_space_param` (raw SpaceParameter enum 0-7) trade constraint
accuracy for CPU; solver settings do not change gravity - configure gravity through
`set_physics_3d_area_param` or project settings. Soft bodies: `create_physics_3d_soft_body`
deforms under forces; assign a mesh with `set_physics_3d_soft_body_mesh`. (4.8: physics
enums moved into scoped namespaces on the engine side; the tools keep the same numeric
values. TODO(verify))

## Navigation maps, regions and paths

The navigation servers follow the same RID pattern: map -> region ->
(3D: navmesh) -> path query. Navigation RIDs come back as `rid` and are never
persisted to scene files.

1. `create_nav_2d_map` / `create_nav_3d_map` - pass `active`: true, maps default to inactive.
   3D extras: `cell_size`, `cell_height` (meters) and `up`; `set_nav_3d_map_cell_size`
   adjusts granularity later - match the cell size baked into the region navmeshes.
2. `create_nav_2d_region` / `create_nav_3d_region` on the map (`map_rid`; optional `enabled`,
   `navigation_layers` bitmask, default 1). Regions define the walkable area - a map with no
   region yields an empty path. For 3D, assign a navmesh with `set_nav_3d_region_navigation_mesh`:
   `mesh_path` is a `res://` path to a `NavigationMesh` resource (`.tres` or `.obj`).
3. Query with `get_nav_2d_map_path` / `get_nav_3d_map_path` (`origin`, `destination`; optional
   `optimize`, `navigation_layers`). Returns `path` as an array of points - empty when the map
   has no baked regions or mesh. `get_nav_3d_map_closest_point_to_segment` snaps a position
   onto the navigation mesh (`start`, `end`, optional `use_collision`).

## Navigation agents and obstacles

- `create_nav_2d_agent` / `create_nav_3d_agent` on a map (`map_rid`, `position`;
  optional `radius`, `max_speed`). Avoidance is off by default - pass
  `avoidance_enabled` (2D) or `use_3d_avoidance` (3D) true to enable it.
- Drive the agent every frame with `set_nav_2d_agent_velocity` /
  `set_nav_3d_agent_velocity`: the agent adjusts the desired velocity around
  obstacles before the value is used for movement.
- `get_nav_3d_agent_state` reads back the registered `position` and the last
  supplied `velocity` - use it to verify the agent is registered.
- `create_nav_3d_obstacle` places an obstacle (`radius`, `height`) that
  avoidance-enabled agents steer around; plain agents ignore it.

## Rendering: 2D canvas items

`create_render_canvas_item` returns the item RID. Draw commands (all take it):
`add_render_canvas_item_rect` (`rect` + `color`; optional `antialiased`),
`add_render_canvas_item_circle`, `add_render_canvas_item_texture_rect` (texture RID from
`create_render_texture_from_image`; optional `tile`, `modulate`, `transpose`) and
`add_render_canvas_item_line`. `set_render_canvas_item_transform` sets axis scaling plus
origin offset; `set_render_canvas_item_visible` is a hard on/off, not a toggle.

## Rendering: scenario, camera, lights, meshes

- `create_render_scenario` hosts cameras, lights, meshes and fog;
  `set_render_scenario_environment` attaches an environment (external RID only -
  no create tool exists).
- `create_render_camera` + `set_render_camera_transform` (only the origin is
  applied - the camera always looks down -Z) + `set_render_camera_perspective`
  (`fovy_degrees` default 75, `z_near` 0.01, `z_far` 4000) or
  `set_render_camera_orthogonal` (uniform `size`, default 10).
- `create_render_light` - `type` "directional" (default), "omni" or "spot";
  `set_render_light_param` takes 0=energy, 1=specular, 2=range, 3=size,
  4=attenuation (`range` only affects omni and spot); `set_render_light_color`
  takes a color, alpha ignored.
- `create_render_mesh` holds geometry; `add_render_mesh_surface` adds a surface
  from arrays (`primitive` defaults to triangles; surfaces index from 0 in call
  order). `create_render_material` + `set_render_material_param` set named shader
  parameters (`type_hint` controls Variant decoding);
  `set_render_mesh_surface_material` assigns a material RID to one surface. Known
  gap: **no tool attaches a shader to a material** - materials only take effect
  with external shader setup such as `code_execute`.

## Rendering: viewports, particles, environment, shaders, textures

- `create_render_viewport` + `set_render_viewport_size` (default 640x480) +
  `set_render_viewport_clear_mode` (0=always, 1=never, 2=only_next_frame). No tool
  can attach a camera or canvas to a viewport, so standalone viewports cannot be
  rendered on their own - mainly useful for external composition.
- `create_render_particles` (`mode` 0=2D, 1=3D) + `set_render_particles_emitting`,
  `set_render_particles_lifetime` (seconds, default 1.0) and
  `restart_render_particles` (fresh emission cycle for one-shot bursts). No tool
  instantiates particles into a scenario.
- Environment tools all take an `environment_rid` from an external source (no create tool
  exists): `set_render_environment_bg_color`, `set_render_environment_ambient_light`
  (`source` 0=bg, 1=disabled, 2=color, 3=sky, plus `energy` - fills shadows so unlit
  surfaces stay visible), `set_render_environment_glow` (bloom),
  `set_render_environment_ssr`, `set_render_environment_tonemap`,
  `set_render_environment_sdfgi`, `set_render_environment_volumetric_fog`.
  `create_render_fog_volume` + `set_render_fog_volume_shape` add localized fog volumes
  (visible when the environment has volumetric fog enabled).
- `create_render_shader` (optional `code` at creation) and
  `set_render_shader_code` replace the source (compilation happens server-side).
  `set_render_shader_parameter_global` sets a global shader parameter - the shader
  must declare it with the `global` keyword. `create_render_texture_from_image`
  loads a texture RID from `res://`, `user://` or absolute image paths; relative
  paths are not supported.
- `create_render_sky` + `set_render_sky_material` (material RID defines the
  appearance; no tool attaches a sky to an environment); `create_render_decal` and
  `create_render_reflection_probe` have no instantiation tools yet;
  `set_render_instance_visible` / `set_render_instance_layer_mask` control
  server-side instances (instance RIDs must come from an external source).

## TextServer: fonts and shaped text

1. `create_text_font` returns the font RID every font tool requires.
   `set_text_font_data` loads a `.ttf`/`.otf`/`.woff2` file path;
   `get_text_font_system_path` resolves an installed system font (`font_name`,
   optional `weight` default 400, `stretch` default 100, `italic`) to an absolute
   path you can pass as `data` directly.
2. `set_text_font_antialiasing` (0=none, 1=gray, 2=grayscale, 3=subpixel; use 0
   for pixel-art fonts) and `set_text_font_hinting` (0=none, 1=light, 2=normal -
   light is the typical UI default) apply after `set_text_font_data` so they
   affect the loaded font.
3. `has_text_feature` checks TextServer capabilities before relying on them:
   1=simple_layout, 2=bidi_layout, 4=shaped, 8=kerning, 16=ligatures.
4. Shaped measurement: `create_shaped_text` (`direction` 0=auto, 1=ltr, 2=rtl;
   `orientation` 0=horizontal, 1=vertical) -> `add_shaped_text_string` (font configured
   first, `size` in pixels, optional `language` improves shaping) ->
   `get_shaped_text_size` returns the pixel dimensions - zero until strings are added;
   use it to size labels before creating them. `is_text_locale_right_to_left` (BCP-47
   in, boolean out) picks alignment or `direction` before shaping RTL text.

## Minimal workflows

2D ray query against the open scene (space auto-detected):

```json
{"name": "intersect_physics_2d_ray", "arguments": {"from": {"x": 0, "y": 0}, "to": {"x": 100, "y": 200}}}
```

Navigation setup and path query (run such sequences in order with `batch_execute`):

```json
{"name": "create_nav_2d_map", "arguments": {"active": true}}
{"name": "create_nav_2d_region", "arguments": {"map_rid": 1}}
{"name": "get_nav_2d_map_path",
 "arguments": {"map_rid": 1, "origin": {"x": 0, "y": 0},
               "destination": {"x": 200, "y": 100}}}
```

## RID lifecycle and silent failure

- **Invalid RIDs fail silently.** Calling any tool - including `free` - on a
  stale, already-freed or never-existing RID neither crashes nor returns an error:
  the server resolves the RID, gets nothing and drops the call. At the tool layer
  this looks like a successful call with no effect. There is no "RID not found"
  error to catch, so track which create call produced which id yourself.
- **Canvas teardown does not cascade.** Freeing a canvas RID does not free the
  canvas items parented to it: their parent pointer is cleared and they become
  orphans that keep existing (and drawing) until freed one by one.
- **Shapes detach automatically.** Freeing a shape RID removes it from every body
  that references it; the bodies themselves are unaffected and stay alive - the
  opposite of the canvas behavior above.
- **No leak reporting.** RIDs leaked at editor exit produce no warning at the
  server layer (only lower-level native rendering-device RIDs get a leak warning).
  Repeatedly creating RIDs without freeing them accumulates silently across a long
  session; everything is reclaimed only when the editor process exits. Object
  creation is two-phase internally (allocate then initialize), invisible at the
  tool level.

## Timing and threads

- **Editor single-thread assumption.** The editor forces single-threaded rendering
  (multi-threaded rendering would crash on startup), so RenderingServer calls made
  on the main thread execute synchronously and immediately. MCP tools can assume
  "the change is in effect by the next draw" - there is no worker thread to wait for.
- **Physics tick order.** Each physics tick runs: state sync -> flush of query
  results (direct-state reads and integration callbacks see the previous step) ->
  node `_physics_process` -> navigation -> message queue flush -> integration step
  -> flush. Node physics callbacks therefore observe the previous step's state.
- **Direct state window and the space lock.** In threaded physics, a direct state object
  fetched outside the sync window returns null with an error, and while a space is
  locked, intersection queries return empty results. Re-entering queries from inside a
  physics callback silently gets nothing; querying from `_physics_process` is safe.
- **Navigation setters are deferred.** Every navigation setter goes through a
  command queue applied at the server's next sync; reading back immediately
  returns the old value, with no error for "not applied yet".
- **Map rebuilds use double-buffered iteration slots.** Region or navmesh changes rebuild
  the map in the other slot at the next sync (possibly asynchronously); slots swap only
  once the rebuild finishes, and if the old slot is still occupied the swap waits another
  round. Poll `map_get_iteration_id` to track rebuild progress (slots exist since 4.7).
- **First query returns an empty path.** Before a map has been synced at least
  once, path queries silently return an empty path in release builds; after
  setting up regions, allow one sync (frame) before trusting an empty result.
- **Nav sync runs twice per frame** - once from process (sync only) and once from
  physics_process (sync + avoidance step + avoidance callbacks). Avoidance-adjusted
  velocities therefore only update on physics ticks.
- **Same-frame ordering.** Each frame runs: node `_process` -> message queue flush ->
  navigation sync -> RenderingServer sync -> draw. A region changed from `_process`
  (e.g. via `code_execute`) is picked up by the same frame's navigation sync, and
  rendering happens after that - friendly to "change it and screenshot immediately".
- Forcing a RenderingServer sync every frame for more than 5 consecutive frames
  logs a persistent warning. Viewports with a dimension of 1px or less silently
  render nothing, and a viewport set to UPDATE_ONCE renders once and then flips
  to disabled.

## See also

- `godot-autopilot-content` - TileMap, animation, audio and UI theming workflows.
- `godot-autopilot-scene-system` - building and editing the scene nodes these RID tools bridge to.
- `godot-autopilot-resources` - saving shape resources as `.tres` for `CollisionShape` assignment.
- `godot-autopilot-scripting` - `code_execute` usage for the external-RID setups.
- `references/tool-reference-physics-nav.md` - the full physics + navigation tool tables.
- `references/tool-reference-rendering.md` - the full render + text tool tables.

# The GDA CLI

Companion reference of the godot-autopilot-tools volume: how to reach the server from a shell — the first-class `gda` channel — through `bunx`, through a globally installed `gda`, or through a self-contained binary that needs no JavaScript runtime at all.

The GDA CLI is the first-class and only scripted calling channel. Every call goes through this command or, when your harness lists them, the native MCP tools; nothing else is sanctioned.

## When this channel applies

The CLI is the default channel: enter here whenever a shell works, whether or not the harness lists native MCP tools. Two situations in particular bring you here:

- **No MCP client is configured.** The user installed the plugin in Godot and the project contains `addons/godot-autopilot`, but the harness has no GDA MCP server wired up, so no GDA tools appear in your tool list.
- **The client lost its tools.** The tool list went empty or calls fail right after an editor restart and reconnecting did not help.

When both a shell and native MCP tools are available, the CLI remains the first-class surface; the native tools are the compatibility face.

## Which distribution to use

Probe the machine before choosing: `bun --version`, then `node --version`.

| Precondition | Distribution | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Bun 1.1 or newer | `bunx` a ref that actually ships the CLI (see the caveat below) | No install; instant once cached |
| Bun, used repeatedly | `bun install -g`, then plain `gda` | One install, zero download afterwards |
| Neither Bun nor Node | Standalone binary from the Release page | One download per version |

All three distributions are the same program: they speak the same MCP protocol, accept the same subcommands and share the same exit codes. Nothing in the calling protocol changes when you switch.

**Caveat — the pinned ref resolves only once its tag is published.** As of `0.3.1` the repository tree does ship the CLI: the root `package.json` exposes the `gda` binary as `cli/bin/gda.ts`, and `cli/` is part of the tree, so `bunx "github:jesspig/Godot-Autopilot#0.3.1"` resolves the `gda` binary as soon as the `0.3.1` tag exists on the remote. The older caveat — that the pinned tag was cut before the CLI existed, carried no `cli/` directory and no root `package.json`, and could never resolve — no longer applies to the current pin. What still applies is the publishing step: until the `0.3.1` tag and its release are out, that ref is not fetchable, so use `bunx "github:jesspig/Godot-Autopilot#develop" <cmd>` in the meantime (that branch does ship the CLI, but it is an unreleased moving target rather than a pinned version, so pin your own copy with `bun install -g` if you need a stable one). The versioned alternative is the standalone binary below: each release publishes the `gda` assets for five targets next to `addons.zip` with a `sha256sums.txt`, so check the release page for the asset and verify the checksum before downloading.

## Commands

Offline family — these work with no running instance and no MCP client:

| Command | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `skills list` | List the bundled skill books with their paths and file counts |
| `skills show <name>` | Print one skill book's SKILL.md; `--file <rel>` reads a reference file instead |
| `tools list` / `tools search <query>` / `tools describe <tool>` | Offline tool catalog from the cached `/api/tools` snapshot |
| `projects` | List known Godot projects from the plugin and CLI registries |

Example — no running instance and no MCP client required:

```
gda skills list
[{"name":"godot-autopilot","path":".../skills/godot-autopilot","files":2}, ... 9 books]

gda skills show godot-autopilot-tools
---
name: godot-autopilot-tools
description: "Calling the GDA (godot-autopilot) plugin: ..."

gda tools list
{"generated_at":"2026-11-10T07:00:00.000Z","version":"0.3.1","tools":[{"name":"create_scene_node",...}, ...]}

gda tools search capture
{"generated_at":"...","version":"0.3.1","tools":[{"name":"capture_editor_viewport",...}]}
```
The `tools` family reads a catalog cached by the last successful `gda api list` (or a fresh `gda tools ... --refresh`), so it works with no running instance.

Calling family — meta tools are called directly, every domain tool goes through `call_tool`:

| Command | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ping` | Health check; safest first call |
| `status` | Server status and project info |
| `categories` | List all tool categories |
| `search <query>` | Search tools by keyword (optionally `--category` / `--tags`) |
| `describe <tool>` | Full schema and side-effect marker for one tool |
| `call <tool>` | Execute one tool; arguments via `--args '<json>'` or `--args-file <path>` |

Lifecycle and control family — these manage editor processes or the local control plane:

| Command | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `list` | List instances from both registries, merged: CLI-started entries (`source: "cli"`) plus live plugin-index instances (`source: "plugin"`, deduplicated by pid/port), each with `live`; add `--probe <port>` to append a `source: "probe"` entry for one explicitly probed port (no port scanning) |
| `start` | Launch an editor and wait until its server answers |
| `stop <id>` | Stop an instance. A headless instance has no window to receive a close request, so it is force-stopped directly and reports `method: "force"` — that is expected, not a fallback. A windowed instance is stopped gracefully; `--force` kills it. The instance can also be addressed with `--id`, `--port` or `--project` instead of the positional id |
| `restart <id>` | Stop the instance and start it again on the same port, headless mode and Godot executable. Headless instances (and any instance with `--force`) are force-stopped; windowed instances stop gracefully. Same addressing as `stop`. The stop phase waits a fixed 10 seconds and ignores `--wait`; if a windowed process is still alive, no replacement is started and the registration is kept |
| `serve` | Start the loopback control-plane proxy (default `127.0.0.1:9700`) that routes to one or several instances; see the control-plane section below |
| `logs <id>` | Tail the instance log |

REST family — these do not speak MCP; they call the plugin's plain-HTTP face on the same port:

| Command | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `api list [query]` | List the registered tools through the REST face; `--query`, `--category` and `--tags` filter the result |
| `api describe <tool>` | One tool's schema and side-effect marker, through the REST face |
| `api call <tool>` | Call one tool through the REST face; `--args` or `--args-file` carry the argument object, which is the request body itself |
| `endpoints` | Show the discovered MCP and REST endpoints, the port they came from, and whether the port is alive |

The REST commands need a bearer token; the CLI reads it from the plugin's instance registry and attaches it. When no instance record is found the command fails with a transport error naming the port and its source, and points at the registry path. `--probe` picks the liveness check: `light` (a TCP connect, the default) or `strict` (TCP plus one HTTP request). The endpoint contract and the token sources are in references/rest-api.md.

Follow the same discovery order as the native channel: `ping`, then `search` or `categories`, then `describe`, then `call`. Calling with an unknown name fails with a message telling you to search — never guess names.

## Global options

`--port` (default 9527; 9700 for `serve`), `--id`, `--project`, `--pretty`, `--raw`, `--timeout`, `--category`, `--tags`, `--args`, `--args-file`, `--save-images`, `--godot`, `--headless`, `--play`, `--no-import`, `--wait`, `--force`, `--tail`, `--bind`, `--no-auth`, `--query`, `--probe`, `--help`, `--version`.

`--bind` and `--no-auth` apply to `serve` only; `--bind` takes a loopback address and `--no-auth` turns the control-plane token check off. `--query` applies to the `api list` subcommand only. `--probe` is overloaded: `light`/`strict` liveness level for `api`, `endpoints` and `start`, or a port number (1-65535) for `list` to probe exactly that port; passing it to another command is a usage error.

`--quiet` was removed and is no longer recognized. Passing it now fails with exit code 3 and the message "unknown option: --quiet", and it is gone from `gda --help`. An older wrapper that still passes `--quiet` will start failing — drop the flag rather than working around it. Diagnostics already go to stderr on their own, so the flag bought nothing.

`--id`, `--port` and `--project` are mutually exclusive, and `stop` and `restart` accept a positional instance id as a fourth way to address an instance; passing a positional id together with any of the three options is a usage error. Every project path in that chain is normalized with `path.resolve` semantics, so the same relative `--project` (for example `../x`) now resolves to the same instance under `ping`, `stop`, `restart` and `list` alike. Before, those commands disagreed on the same input and could address different instances.

## Port and target resolution

Never assume the default port. The plugin may have moved off 9527 when that port was already taken: an editor that finds 9527 occupied picks the next free port in a fixed range instead. The target is resolved in seven steps, and each step records where the port came from:

| Priority | Source | What to read |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `--port` | The port you pass |
| 2 | `--id` | The instance id in the registry; the instance must still be alive |
| 3 | `GODOT_AUTOPILOT_PORT` environment variable | The port it holds |
| 4 | CLI registry | A live instance registered for `--project`, or for the current directory |
| 5 | Plugin instance registry | The plugin's own registry of running instances, matched by project path - this is where the REST token comes from too |
| 6 | Project server-ready trace and config.json | The port recorded by the project under the Godot user data folder |
| 7 | Fallback | 9527 |

`gda endpoints` prints the resolved port together with the step it came from, both endpoint views and the liveness result - that is the quickest way to find out where a port came from. The trace and the config file live under the Godot user data folder of the project. Pass `--port` explicitly whenever you already know the editor was configured with a custom port.

## Passing arguments

Domain calls carry the domain tool name plus its arguments object. Give the arguments inline with `--args`, or from a JSON file with `--args-file`:

```
gda call <tool> --args '{"type": "Node2D", "name": "Player", "parent_path": "Root/Actors"}'
gda call <tool> --args-file args.json
```

args.json holds the arguments object, for example:

```json
{"type": "Node2D", "name": "Player", "parent_path": "Root/Actors"}
```

`--args` and `--args-file` apply to the `call` command only; passing them to another command is a usage error. An unreadable or malformed arguments file is a usage error too, not a transport error.

## Engine resolution for `start`

`start` needs the Godot executable. It resolves `--godot` first, then a PATH lookup (`godot.exe`/`godot4.exe` on Windows, `godot`/`godot4` elsewhere). If neither hits, it fails with `cannot locate the Godot executable (pass --godot or put godot on PATH)`.

The `GODOT_PATH` environment variable is **not** read, and neither is a `.env` in the project: that variable exists only for the L2 engine test runner. When the user's engine is not on PATH, pass `--godot` explicitly with the absolute path they gave you.

## Session and lifecycle behaviour

- **A failed start is rolled back.** When the readiness probe fails, `start` terminates the editor process it launched and removes the pending log file, then reports the failure. A failed start therefore leaves no orphaned Godot process behind and no half-written log to clean up by hand.
- **A restarted server is picked up again.** The handshake state is tracked per target URL, and a server restart invalidates it. When the server answers a request with the "session not initialized" rejection, the CLI re-handshakes once per URL per process and replays the request. The same CLI process therefore survives an editor restart instead of failing with an HTTP 400 or a -32600 error for the rest of its life.

## Control plane (`gda serve`)

`gda serve` starts a loopback-only proxy that gives one entry point to several editor instances. It is a pure proxy: it does not add tools, does not change any semantics and does not start or stop editors.

- **Listen**: `127.0.0.1:9700` by default. `--port` changes the port; `--bind` accepts loopback addresses only (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `localhost`) and rejects anything else; `--timeout` sets the upstream wait (default 60 seconds).
- **Routes**: `GET /control/health` needs no token. `GET /control/instances` lists live instances (never their tokens) and needs a token. `/i/<ref>/api/...` and `/i/<ref>/mcp` forward to the chosen instance. `<ref>` accepts three forms, matched in this order: the plugin's `instance_id` (for example `gda-daa757f3-9672-1792697320437`), the CLI id `p<pid>` (for example `p9672`, exactly what `gda list` prints, matched by process id), then a numeric port (for example `9530`). Plain `/api/...` and `/mcp` forward to the single live instance; with several live instances they return 409 `instance_ambiguous` with `candidates`, and with none they return 503 `no_active_instance`.
- **Auth**: send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The token is generated on first start at `<home>/.godot-autopilot/control.token` (64 hex characters, mode `0600`) and reused afterwards. `--no-auth` disables the check with a warning — every local process can then drive the editor.
- **Forwarding**: the proxy drops the client's `Authorization` header, attaches the target instance's own token, and streams the response through unchanged (SSE included), adding `X-GDA-Instance` with the instance that served the call.
- **Not for process control**: there are no HTTP start/stop endpoints by design; use `gda start` / `stop` / `restart` for that.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | Tool failure (the payload carries an error) |
| 2 | Transport or environment failure (connection refused, timeout, HTTP error, missing engine) |
| 3 | Usage error (unknown command, missing argument, bad option) |

A response that carries a top-level JSON-RPC `error` envelope is a tool failure, not a transport failure: it exits 1 and the envelope is printed as the payload. The same holds for a payload that carries an inner error. Exit 2 is reserved for the channel itself being unusable — the server is not listening, the endpoint answered with an HTTP error, or the request timed out. Do not read exit 2 as "the tool returned nothing".

## Output contract

- stdout carries the payload only, as compact JSON; `--pretty` indents it by two spaces.
- `--raw` prints the unprocessed response envelope instead, with image data replaced by a byte-count placeholder.
- Diagnostics go to stderr, prefixed with `[gda]`.
- A tool failure is exit code 1 with the business payload on stdout: read the error object inside the payload, not the transport message.

## Image rules

Screenshot tools (`capture_editor_viewport`, `capture_game_viewport`, `capture_display_screen`) return image payloads. By default the CLI reports image metadata only — mime type and byte count — and writes nothing to disk. Pass `--save-images DIR` to decode the payloads into DIR under self-generated file names (gda_<timestamp>_<index>.png). Inspect the saved files the same way you would inspect image content on the native channel before trusting an edit.

## Standalone binary

The release workflow builds the `gda` binary for five platforms and attaches the assets plus a checksum file to the GitHub release. The binaries are not in every release: the release cut before the `cli` job joined the workflow still carries only the addon package, so check the release page for the asset before you promise a download to the user.

Once a release ships them, assets are named `gda-<version>-<platform>` where platform is one of `windows-x64` (`.zip`, contains `gda.exe`), `linux-x64`, `linux-x64-musl`, `macos-arm64`, `macos-x64` (`.tar.gz`, contains `gda`). Each such release also ships `sha256sums.txt`.

Download the asset that matches the user's OS and CPU from the release page, verify it against the checksum file, then run it exactly like `gda`:

```
sha256sum -c sha256sums.txt --ignore-missing
chmod +x gda
./gda ping
```

Platform notes:

- **macOS** — binaries are ad-hoc signed. If the first launch is blocked by quarantine, clear the attribute with `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ./gda` (or have the user allow it in System Settings). Do not claim the binary is notarized; it is not.
- **Linux** — the plain `linux-x64` asset needs glibc; use `linux-x64-musl` on Alpine or musl-based images.
- **Windows** — unzip and run `gda.exe`. An unsigned binary may trigger a SmartScreen prompt; that is expected.

Prefer `bunx` over the binary whenever Bun exists: it needs no download. It is pinned to the plugin version only once that version's tag is published, so the `develop` ref above moves under you — install your own copy with `bun install -g` when you need a stable CLI.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Meaning | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Connection refused | Editor closed, plugin disabled, or wrong port | Open the editor with the plugin enabled; run `gda endpoints` to see which port was resolved and where it came from; pass `--port` explicitly |
| Timeout (exit 2) | Work unit too large for the wait budget | Split into smaller calls; `--timeout` only extends the client wait, server caps still apply |
| Unknown tool name (exit 1) | Guessed or stale tool name | Discover exact names with `search` and confirm with `describe`; never invent names |
| Authorization denied (exit 1) | The tool's capability is not authorized | Enable it via the `GODOT_AUTOPILOT_ALLOW` environment variable plus engine restart, or the matching MCP Config dock checkbox effective on the next call; write-class tools need `write` |
| No API token available (exit 2) | The plugin's instance registry has no record for that port | Run `gda endpoints` to find the port and its source; the token lives in the plugin instance registry, not in the CLI registry |
| Empty or missing image output | Metadata-only default | Re-run with `--save-images DIR` and inspect the files on disk |
| bunx cannot resolve the CLI | The pinned tag is not published yet (the tree does ship the CLI; the ref only resolves once the tag exists) | Use the `#develop` ref or a global install; see the caveat above |

Tool-level failures (bad arguments, missing nodes) are not transport errors — they arrive as exit code 1 with an error key in the business payload. Handle them with the same error protocol as the native channel: read the watermark, diagnose from real output, confirm the fix by driving the watermark back to 0.

## Hard rules

- **Never hand-write HTTP requests** against the MCP endpoint from any tool. Every MCP call goes through the MCP tools or `gda`. The plugin's REST face has its own reference (references/rest-api.md) and is the one sanctioned place to speak plain HTTP directly.
- **The server binds loopback only.** Never forward its port, never bind it to a public interface, never expose it through a proxy. `gda serve` is the only sanctioned local proxy and is itself loopback-only; it is not a way to reach the server from another machine. The MCP face has no authentication, so the loopback binding is the only thing protecting it; the REST face asks for a bearer token, but that token is a local credential and does not make the port safe to expose.
- **Verify a downloaded binary before executing it.** No checksum match, no run.
- **Report what you actually observed.** Exit code 2 means the channel is down, not that the tool returned nothing; do not fabricate results.

## See also

- godot-autopilot-tools — channel ladder, discovery protocol, error protocol and limits
- references/rest-api.md — the plain-HTTP face: endpoints, token sources and status codes
- references/manual-fallback.md — what to do when no CLI is available either

# Manual Fallback for Godot Autopilot Calls

Companion reference of the godot-autopilot-tools volume: what to do when no automated channel exists. No GDA CLI can run, no native MCP client is available, and the client cannot speak plain HTTP either — hand the work to the user with precise editor instructions instead of reaching for workarounds.

## Trigger criteria

Enter this mode only when at least one holds:

- No usable GDA CLI (no Bun to run it, no way to fetch the standalone binary), no working native MCP client, and no client able to issue plain HTTP requests.
- The harness has no shell at all, so neither the CLI nor the native channel can run.
- The user explicitly asks for manual steps.

If any automated channel works, leave this mode immediately and use it — manual steps are a last resort, not a preference.

## Hard rules

- Stop all automation. Issue no tool calls, run no commands, touch nothing in the project.
- Do not operate the scene on the user's behalf and do not claim an edit was made.
- Do not fabricate call results, log lines, screenshots or watermark values. Anything you did not observe through a real channel does not exist.
- Do not hand-write raw requests against the MCP endpoint from any tool, however urgent the task looks. The ban from the godot-autopilot-tools volume holds here as well. (The plugin's REST face has its own reference and its own examples, but that face needs a token and a client that can issue HTTP requests - neither of which exists in this mode.)
- Keep every instruction inside the editor UI the user already has: menus, docks, inspectors, dialogs. No new software, no config file surgery beyond what the recovery section describes.

## Handoff template

Produce one block per requested change, following this shape:

```
Goal: <one sentence stating the intended outcome>
Why manual: <which trigger criterion applies>

Steps:
1. <menu / dock / button path with exact labels>
2. <value to enter or option to pick, with the field name>
3. <repeat until the change is fully described>

Expected result: <what the user should see when the step worked>
How to verify: <where to look — panel, inspector value, log line, viewport>
If it fails: <the most likely cause and the corrected step>

Information needed back:
- <answer, screenshot, or log excerpt required to continue>
```

Fill every section. A template with an empty verification or an empty information-needed-back section is incomplete — the round trip stalls without them.

## Limits you must declare

State these up front in the handoff so the user can calibrate expectations:

- No live scene access: you cannot read the current scene tree, selection or inspector values. Ask the user to report or screenshot anything you would normally read with `search_tools` discovery, `property_get` or `get_scene_tree`.
- No screenshots: you cannot capture the editor or game viewport. Ask the user to attach one when appearance matters.
- No logs: you cannot read the debugger, engine or plugin output. Ask the user to paste the relevant lines when diagnosis depends on them.
- No watermark confirmation: the error-watermark loop from the godot-autopilot-tools volume cannot run. The user confirms each step against the Expected result line instead.
- No batching across steps: each manual step is confirmed by the user before you describe the next dependent one. Never chain five unverified edits in a single message.

## Recovery — restoring automation

Close every handoff with the shortest applicable path back to an automated channel:

1. Restore the CLI. Install Bun and run the `gda` command (through `bunx` or a global install), or fetch the standalone binary, then use it per references/cli-access.md. No client reconfiguration needed — the CLI is the first-class channel.
2. Restore the native MCP channel. In the editor, open the plugin MCP Config dock and use the Generate button: it writes a project-level MCP configuration for the client in use (twenty clients covered). Restart or reconnect the client harness afterwards — a lost tool list right after an editor restart is a harness reconnect problem, not a server problem.
3. Clear authorization denials on the way back. Script execution needs the `code_execute` capability, game-runtime tools need `game_runtime`, user-registered dynamic tools need `user_tools`, write-class tools need `write`, and destructive tools need `destructive`. Each can be enabled via the `GODOT_AUTOPILOT_ALLOW` environment variable plus an engine restart, or via the matching MCP Config dock checkbox ("Allow code_execute", "Allow game_runtime", "Allow user tools", "Allow write", "Allow destructive"), which takes effect on the next tool call. Un-ticking a box removes only that capability. When the environment variable is set it wins over the dock setting.

## See also

- godot-autopilot-tools — channel ladder, discovery protocol, error protocol and limits
- references/cli-access.md — the CLI to return to first

# The REST API

Companion reference of the godot-autopilot-tools volume: the plain-HTTP face of the plugin, for clients that cannot speak the MCP protocol.

The plugin listens on **one** port and serves two faces on it. The `gda` CLI is the first-class calling surface; the MCP face is the compatibility channel for harnesses that list native tools. The REST face is the alternative for a client that can only issue ordinary HTTP requests — no MCP handshake, no session, no JSON-RPC framing.

This is an **interface reference**, not a new scripted channel. The only scripted calling channel remains the `gda` CLI (see references/cli-access.md). The two snippets below show the shape of a REST call; when a shell is available, prefer `gda api`.

## When this face applies

Enter here when either holds:

- **The client cannot do an MCP handshake.** It can send HTTP requests with a bearer token but has no MCP client, no session handling and no JSON-RPC framing. Some HTTP-first agent harnesses and simple integrations land here.
- **You need a plain probe.** `GET /api/health` answers without a token and returns only liveness, the service version, the bound port and the process id.

If the harness lists native GDA tools, use them. If a shell is available, use the CLI. This face is for the remaining case.

## Endpoints

The path prefix is `/api`. All of them need `Authorization: Bearer <token>` **except** the health probe.

| Method | Path | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api` | Service name, version and the endpoint list |
| GET | `/api/tools` | The registered tools; filter with `query`, `category`, `tags`; page with `limit` and `offset` |
| GET | `/api/tools/<tool>` | One tool's description, category, tags, side-effect marker and input schema |
| POST | `/api/tools/<tool>` | Call one tool — **the request body is the argument object itself** |
| POST | `/api/batch` | Call several tools in order |
| GET | `/api/health` | Liveness probe — **no token required** |
| GET | `/api/openapi.json` | The OpenAPI document for the face |

The tool name in the path may be percent-encoded; only letters, digits, underscore, hyphen and dot are accepted.

## Calling a tool

The body **is** the argument object. There is no `name` / `arguments` wrapper on this face, unlike the MCP `call_tool` meta tool.

```json
{"type": "Node2D", "name": "Player", "parent_path": "Root/Actors"}
```

An empty body means "no arguments". A body that is not a JSON object is rejected with 400. Extra keys that the schema does not declare are ignored rather than rejected; a missing required key or a wrong type is an error.

Batch bodies carry an ordered operation list:

```json
{
  "operations": [
    {"tool": "create_scene_node", "args": {"type": "Node2D", "name": "Player"}},
    {"tool": "property_set", "args": {"path": "Root/Player", "property": "position", "value": {"x": 1, "y": 2}}}
  ],
  "stop_on_error": true
}
```

A batch always answers 200. Per-operation outcomes live in the `results` array: each entry carries the tool name, a status, and either the payload or an error. When `stop_on_error` is true the first failure stops the run and the remaining operations are not executed; the response then says how many ran and how many were skipped.

## Getting the token

The token is a 32-byte random value in hexadecimal (64 lowercase hex characters). Three ways to get it, in order of precedence:

1. **The `gda` CLI does it for you.** `gda api list`, `gda api describe <tool>` and `gda api call <tool>` read the token from the plugin's instance registry and attach the header. This is the recommended path.
2. **Read it from the instance registry.** The plugin writes one record per running instance into `instances.json` under the GDA home directory (the `.godot-autopilot` folder in the user's home directory; set `GODOT_AUTOPILOT_HOME` to move it). Each record's **api_token** field holds the bearer token for that instance, and the same record names the port the instance actually bound.
3. **Read the token file.** The plugin also writes the token into the per-project storage folder as a file named **api_token**. On POSIX the file is tightened to owner-only permissions; on Windows it inherits the ACL of the GDA home directory.

If the editor was started with the `GODOT_AUTOPILOT_API_TOKEN` environment variable set, that value is the token and no file is written.

Never print the token into a log, a commit, or a chat transcript. Treat it like a local credential.

## Status codes

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | Success — including a batch whose individual operations failed | Read the payload |
| 400 | Bad request: malformed body, missing `operations`, bad `limit` or `offset`, bad tool arguments | Fix the request; do not retry unchanged |
| 401 | No token, wrong header shape, or a token that does not match | Read the token again from the instance registry |
| 403 | The tool's capability is not authorized | Enable the capability; see the authorization note below |
| 404 | Unknown route or unknown tool name | Discover the tool name first; never guess |
| 405 | The route does not accept this method | Use the method from the endpoint table |
| 409 | Conflicting request | Retry later |
| 413 | The request body is too large | Split the payload |
| 422 | The tool itself failed | Read the error text; the call reached the tool |
| 429 | Rate limited | Retry in a moment |
| 500 | Internal error | Check the plugin log |
| 503 | The editor is exporting, or the main-thread queue is unavailable | Wait for the export to finish, or retry later for the queue |
| 504 | The editor main thread did not finish inside its budget | **Do not retry blindly** — see below |

A failure body carries an `error` string and a `code` string. Branch on the code, not on the wording.

Two retries deserve care. The main-thread timeout code is marked as cancelled and as **not retryable**: the call was abandoned, but the side effect may still land in the editor afterwards. Read the editor state before deciding to send it again. The queue-unavailable code **is** retryable — that one means the channel itself was momentarily busy.

## Python, minimal

Standard library only; no third-party package needed.

```python
import json
import os
import urllib.request

BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:9527/api"
TOKEN = os.environ["GDA_API_TOKEN"]


def call(method, path, payload=None):
    body = None if payload is None else json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8")
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        BASE + path,
        data=body,
        method=method,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
        return json.loads(response.read().decode("utf-8"))


print(call("GET", "/health"))  # the health probe needs no token
print(call("GET", "/tools?query=scene"))
print(call("POST", "/tools/create_scene_node", {"type": "Node2D", "name": "Player"}))
```

## JavaScript, minimal

`fetch` is built in on Node 18+ and on Bun; no package needed.

```javascript
const BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:9527/api";
const TOKEN = process.env.GDA_API_TOKEN;

async function call(method, path, payload) {
  const response = await fetch(BASE + path, {
    method,
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${TOKEN}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: payload === undefined ? undefined : JSON.stringify(payload),
  });
  return await response.json();
}

console.log(await call("GET", "/health"));
console.log(await call("GET", "/tools?query=scene"));
console.log(await call("POST", "/tools/create_scene_node", { type: "Node2D", name: "Player" }));
```

## Authorization on this face

A valid token proves who is calling; it does not grant anything. The capability gate still applies, and it is checked on every call:

- **Read** tools — those whose side effect is `none` — are allowed by default.
- **Write** tools — `writes_file`, `writes_config`, `shows_alert`, `modifies_window`, `writes_scene` — are **denied by default**. They need the `write` capability in the allow list.
- **Danger** tools — `process`, `code_execute`, `game_runtime`, `destructive` — are denied by default and need their own capability.

Enable a capability with the `GODOT_AUTOPILOT_ALLOW` environment variable (a comma-separated list, or `all`) and an engine restart, or with the matching checkbox in the plugin's MCP Config dock ("Allow code_execute", "Allow game_runtime", "Allow user tools", "Allow write", "Allow destructive"), which saves to the plugin config and takes effect on the next call with no restart. Un-ticking a box removes only that one capability. A denied call answers 403 and names the capability it needs — a write-class call answers 403 authorization_required unless `write` is allowed. This face cannot widen the allow list per request — there is no field in the body that does that.

## Hard rules

- **Loopback only.** The server binds `127.0.0.1`. Never forward the port, never proxy it, never bind it to a public interface.
- **The token is a local credential.** It only works together with the loopback binding. Do not forward it, do not log it, do not commit it.
- **Discover before calling.** Read the tool list first; the tool names in this reference are examples, and the real set is whatever the tool list returns.
- **A timeout is not a retry signal.** Read the editor state before repeating a call that ended in a main-thread timeout.

## See also

- godot-autopilot-tools — channel ladder, discovery protocol, error protocol and limits
- references/cli-access.md — the `gda` CLI, including the REST subcommands and the port resolution chain
